strengths: Addresses a practical and important problem: learning from corrupted data without access to clean samples, with clear applications in medical imaging and scientific discovery
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple corruption types and both natural and scientific imaging domains, with thorough appendices and implementation details
Provides theoretical justification through Theorem 1 showing eigenspace recovery under linear regime, grounding the approach mathematically
Introduces proximal FID as a useful metric for model selection when clean data is unavailable
Strong qualitative results demonstrating high-quality reconstructions across diverse tasks
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (Ambient Tweedie, Ambient Diffusion, score distillation) without introducing fundamentally new methods or insights; contribution feels incremental

Significant gap between theory and practice: Theorem 1 relies on restrictive assumptions (linear low-rank data distribution, perfect score estimation, rank-1 analysis) that don't hold for natural images or practical settings; the link between eigenspace recovery and high-fidelity generation quality is unclear

Modest experimental improvements with limited baselines: improvements over existing corruption-aware baselines are often marginal (e.g., Table 2 shows only 2.5 FID points improvement in some cases); missing comparisons with alternative inverse problem solvers or other distillation techniques

Evaluation concerns: FID computed on corrupted dataset rather than clean data is suboptimal for assessing restoration quality; validity of proximal FID as a reliable proxy metric is not thoroughly validated; no perceptual quality assessment (LPIPS, user studies)

Limited scope and generalizability: primarily evaluated on low-resolution face images (CelebA-HQ); MRI results presented qualitatively without comparison to task-specific reconstruction methods; unclear real-world competitiveness
Reproducibility barriers: requires 8 A100 GPUs with 80GB memory; many hyperparameter choices lack justification; code not provided; substantial implementation burden

Insufficient ablation studies and analysis: missing ablations on distillation loss formulations, sensitivity to hyperparameters, failure mode analysis, and comparison of learned features between one-step and teacher models

Gap between claims and evidence: paper claims method 'consistently surprises' baselines but improvements are often within noise margins; theoretical result presented as strong justification despite practical inapplicability

strengths: Comprehensive and rigorous experimental validation across multiple datasets (CelebA-HQ, FastMRI) with diverse corruption types (Gaussian blur, random imputation, super-resolution) and corruption intensities, demonstrating consistent and significant improvements
Practical significance addressing the important and realistic problem of learning from corrupted data without clean data access, relevant to medical imaging, astronomy, and inverse problems
Significant computational efficiency gains: achieves ~20x speedup via one-step generation and more efficient training (~12M distillation iterations after pretraining)
Flexible and general framework compatible with multiple corruption-aware pretraining objectives (Ambient Tweedie, Ambient Diffusion, Fourier-space variants), extending DSD beyond standard denoising

Theoretical contribution (Theorem 1) providing principled interpretation of score distillation as implicit recovery of clean data covariance eigenspace in linear regime, offering mechanistic understanding
Novel proximal FID metric providing practical model selection criterion for scenarios with unavailable clean validation data—pragmatic contribution addressing real-world constraints

Excellent presentation with clear motivation, logical flow, and strong use of visualizations; extensive appendices with detailed algorithms, implementation details, training curves, and ablations facilitating reproducibility
Rigorous experimental design with appropriate baseline selection, proper ablations on corruption parameters, fair comparisons between underspecified and supervised settings
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: primarily integrates existing techniques (corruption-aware diffusion training from prior work [8,9,11] + score distillation from [6]); the extension to broader corruptions is relatively straightforward rather than fundamentally new

Significant theory-practice gap: Theorem 1 restricted to rank-1 case 'for simplicity' despite images having much higher intrinsic dimensionality; assumes perfect score estimation (unrealistic) and applies only to linear models with low-rank data; no analysis of why/when insights transfer to nonlinear neural networks used in practice

Incomplete baseline comparisons: limited evaluation against recent one-step/few-step generation methods (Consistency Models, Progressive Distillation); primarily compares RSD generator against teacher diffusion rather than other fast sampling approaches; missing domain-specific medical imaging baselines for MRI experiments

Proximal FID metric validity concerns: effectiveness demonstrated only empirically and inconsistently; Table 6 shows cases with noticeable FID divergence between proximal and true FID; correlation with true FID not quantified; limited analysis of failure modes

Understated computational cost analysis: claims efficiency but doesn't clearly separate Phase 1 training cost (still 100M iterations, same as baseline) from Phase 2 distillation cost (12M); total cost comparison versus baseline approaches needs clarification; Table 5 only reports inference time

Limited scope and incomplete ablations: scientific imaging evaluation only on fastMRI (missing other modalities); missing ablations on choice of Fisher divergence over KL in Eq. 11, distillation hyperparameter sensitivity, and controlled comparison of different corruption-aware objectives; Assumption 3 about low-rank generator structure not justified

Weak analysis of score matching in corrupted regime: doesn't deeply analyze how well Phase 1 learns to match corrupted distribution's score despite this being crucial for approach success; no empirical validation of this assumption

Reproducibility gaps: code availability not mentioned; hyperparameter choices may be dataset-dependent; 100M iteration training expensive to reproduce; some implementation details remain underspecified (e.g., sensitivity map initialization in MRI)

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem of learning generative models from corrupted observations without clean ground truth, with applications to scientific and medical imaging.
Provides a unified framework handling multiple corruption types (denoising, inpainting, super-resolution, Fourier-space masking) within a single methodology.
Includes extensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets (CIFAR-10, CelebA-HQ, AFHQ-v2, multi-coil MRI) with thorough ablations.
Provides theoretical analysis with Wasserstein distance bounds in linear Gaussian settings, adding some rigor to the approach.
Demonstrates empirical improvements in image quality metrics (FID) and offers comprehensive implementation details in appendices.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Phase I applies existing corruption-aware diffusion losses from recent works (Daras et al., Bai et al., Xie et al.), while Phase II directly uses standard score distillation (Zhou et al. 2024) with minimal modification. The contribution is primarily an engineering application rather than methodological advance.

Weak experimental baselines and unfair comparisons: Tables primarily compare against teacher model variants rather than state-of-the-art corruption-aware methods. Recent baselines (EM-Diffusion, Ambient Diffusion) appear to use different experimental settings, making direct comparison invalid. Domain-specific baselines for MRI are absent.

Significant disconnect between theory and practice: Theoretical analysis (Section F) assumes low-rank linear models with strong structural assumptions that don't match practical high-resolution image restoration. The theory doesn't explain why the method works with non-linear networks. Bounds become loose with multiple corruptions.

Overstated speedup claims: The 30× speedup is expected from multi-step→one-step distillation and doesn't reflect a novel contribution. Hidden pretraining costs (~4 hours on CIFAR-10) are not clearly factored into practical cost-benefit analysis. Speedup is measured with batch size 1024 on specific hardware, limiting generalizability.

Marginal improvements in many settings: Data efficiency improvements diminish with more data (Table 5). Conditional inverse problem results show modest gains (2-3%, Table 9). Teacher-truncated baselines are artificially weak, inflating RSD's apparent advantages.

Proximal FID model selection is ad-hoc and unjustified: Computing FID on corrupted training samples as a proxy for true FID lacks theoretical grounding. No analysis of when this proxy is reliable or how it guards against overfitting to the corruption type.

Limited handling of unknown corruption level: Proposed solutions (off-the-shelf estimation or calibration) are heuristic without principled justification. Results degrade significantly with unknown σ (Tables 14-15), revealing a real practical limitation.

Incomplete experimental analysis: No failure mode analysis or discussion of when standard diffusion is preferable. Random noise ablation claims 'stability' but shows clear degradation (Table 17). Conditional inverse problem evaluation limited to denoising only.

Presentation issues: Title 'beyond acceleration' is vague and misleading regarding actual contributions. Related work underemphasizes that this builds directly on recent corruption-aware diffusion literature. Key algorithmic details are relegated to appendices.

strengths: Well-motivated and practically important problem: learning from corrupted data is valuable for scientific imaging where clean observations are scarce
Unified framework handling diverse corruption operators (blur, downsampling, masking, Fourier operations) elegantly within single approach
Strong experimental results with consistent improvements over baselines across all tasks and substantial 30× inference speedup
Comprehensive experimental evaluation including ablations on data scale, noise levels, and distillation losses across multiple datasets (natural and medical imaging)
Solid theoretical contributions establishing conditions under which distillation preserves generation quality with clear assumptions and extensions
Practical efficiency analysis demonstrating Phase II distillation requires only ~4 hours with significant inference-time improvements (20 seconds vs ~10 minutes)
Comprehensive implementation details and reproducibility commitment with clear algorithmic descriptions and training protocols
Clear problem formulation and well-structured presentation making contributions accessible
weaknesses: Limited theoretical scope: main theorems assume linear Gaussian settings with low-rank structure, restrictive for high-dimensional image synthesis; gap between theory and practice not fully bridged
Incomplete baseline comparisons: primarily compares to corruption-aware diffusion and distilled diffusion; limited comparison to other recent one-step methods or supervised restoration approaches

Method complexity and design choices: two-phase pipeline more complex than alternatives; some design choices inadequately justified (e.g., why specific Phase I objectives); limited failure mode analysis
Assumes known corruption operator, limiting applicability when corruption characteristics are unknown or misspecified; no robustness analysis provided
Limited generalization analysis: no cross-corruption generalization explored; transferability to distribution shifts or new corruption types unknown
Computational cost not fully contextualized: Phase I still requires substantial computation (100-200M iterations); total cost not compared to supervised restoration baselines
Missing key experiments on cross-corruption transfer, robustness to corruption misspecification, and comparison of total training time against supervised alternatives
Paper length (68 pages) with important content relegated to appendices; some limitations discussed only in appendix should be in main text
